title: The self that blames itself

segments.voice: Yesterday: tamnun tastakthir, and your line, give, don't count. Did a gift go out with no string on it, and stay out of the conversation? Today a new surah, al-Qiyamah, and an oath by something inside you. Day six hundred fifty-seven.

You said something sharp at dinner. Everyone moved on. But at eleven at night, brushing your teeth, a small voice starts up: that wasn't fair. You should apologize. Why did you say that? Nobody else heard it. Nobody else needed to. That voice, the one that won't let you off the hook, is ordinary enough to go unnoticed. The Qur'an notices it. At the start of surah seventy-five, it swears by it, right next to the Day of Resurrection.

Surah al-Qiyamah opens with two oaths. Verse one: I swear by the Day of Resurrection. Verse two, in Pickthall's translation: "Nay, I swear by the accusing soul (that this Scripture is true)." The Arabic is an-nafs al-lawwamah. Nafs is the self, the soul, the inner person. Lawwamah is an intensive form from lawm, blame: the self that blames, and keeps blaming, again and again. Why put it next to the Day of Resurrection? Commentators have suggested that the conscience is a small preview of that day. A reckoning that happens inside you, every evening, long before the final one. Muslim writers later drew a map of the self from three Qur'anic phrases. An-nafs al-ammarah, in surah Yusuf: the self that urges toward wrong. An-nafs al-lawwamah, here: the self that blames itself afterward. And an-nafs al-mutma'innah, in surah al-Fajr: the self at peace, called home to its Lord. Some teachers describe these as stages, or as three voices everyone hears at different times. Al-Hasan al-Basri, an early scholar of Basra, is reported to have said that a believer is always taking himself to account, while a careless person moves ahead without looking back. Notice what the blaming self is not. It isn't despair, and it isn't self-hatred. In the map, it's a good sign, a step up from the self that only urges. It's the part of you that still cares about the truth. The verse honors it with an oath. In that map, the aim is to listen to it, make things right, and move toward the peace after it.

The practice: notice your conscience. Sit, and walk back through the last day. Wait for the place where the small voice speaks up: that wasn't fair, that wasn't true, that wasn't kind. Don't argue with it, and don't pile on. Just hear what it's actually saying. Then ask it one question: what would make this right? Let the answer be small and doable. The bell holds the time.
Lawwamah: an intensive form from lawm, blame, the self that blames and keeps blaming, honored with an oath in 75:2. Today's word.
Your line: the voice that blames. Today, when it speaks up, treat it like a friend with bad news: listen, thank it, and do the small thing it asked. Day six hundred fifty-seven.

howItsDone: Some Muslims practice muhasabah, taking oneself to account, often at night, reviewing the day's words and deeds; teachers describe the self in three states drawn from the Qur'an: urging to wrong, self-blaming, and at peace.

original.note: Arabic, 75:2: the self that blames itself. lawwamah, an intensive form from lawm, blame.

trapdoor: what it means: the conscience that calls you back after a wrong, honored by an oath beside the Day of Resurrection.
what a scholar hears: lawwamah is intensive (blaming again and again); with 12:53 and 89:27 it forms the classic three states of the nafs.
